🚨 Every $TAO subnet has been forced to run the same business model. eTAO ends that.

It's one of the biggest changes to subnet economics since dTAO. Watch the 80-second explainer 🎬👇

How it worked until now

Every 12 seconds, each subnet mints new alpha tokens. Almost every subnet split them the exact same way:

• 18% to the owner (the team running it)
• 41% to validators and their stakers (checking the work)
• 41% to miners (doing the work)

A GPU farm, a research lab and a consumer app all lived by one rule.

What eTAO (Expressive TAO) changes

Each subnet owner can now set their own split, within limits:

• Miners: at least 33%
• Validators: up to 50%
• Owners: up to 33% (18% minimum for lease-created subnets)
• Changes about once a week

Total emissions don't change. eTAO only changes where they go.

Why that's a big deal

Different businesses need different budgets:

• A compute subnet short on GPUs pays miners more
• A research team funds its developers through the owner share
• A subnet with hard-to-check work spends more on validators

Targon (SN4) is the live example. In the Talking Targon episode with Const, the team said customers want more compute than it has, and most of it is rented.

Push miners from 41% to 80% and miners get about 95% more tokens. At the same token price, that nearly doubles the budget to bring on GPUs.

More compute → more revenue → bigger buybacks. That's Targon's plan, not a guarantee.

The twist

Lower yield can be bullish.

A high APY tells you how fast new tokens reach stakers. It doesn't tell you what customers pay.

Normal companies make this trade every day: reinvest in production instead of paying out. eTAO lets subnets make the same call.

The guardrails

• Root $TAO stakers are paid their baseline first, calculated from live chain state
• Owners can't set validators below that baseline
• Miners can never drop below a third
• The burn and recycle slots exist but are fixed at zero for now

Why? Const explained it: without a floor, a subnet could cut out its outside holders, fake its price signal and pull emissions it hasn't earned. The floor keeps every subnet paying the network that funds it.

Everything else that just changed

eTAO isn't alone. Bittensor is redesigning itself fast:

• Null Consensus: opt-in, up to 2,500 participant slots per subnet, up from 256
• Proof-of-work registration: miners can join with compute, no TAO upfront
• Subnet registration cost now halves every 8 days, down from 16
• New-subnet immunity drops from 120 days to 60
• Gamma (in development): subnets buy compute, storage and inference from each other with their emissions

Put it together: bigger competitions, easier entry, faster turnover, custom budgets, and soon an internal economy where subnets are each other's customers.

The take

• eTAO is on testnet now. Mainnet comes with the next runtime upgrade (v481)
• An owner can fund the wrong thing. A weak scoring system can pay miners who farm rewards instead of building the product
• Alpha staking yields aren't permanent. A subnet's split is now part of what you're investing in
• Emissions aren't revenue. The bull case only works if extra output gets paid for

Why it matters for AI

AI doesn't grow in straight lines. Agents make thousands of requests while a person reviews one dashboard. Workloads shift from compute to storage to verification in weeks.

A network funding that can't run on one fixed rule.

Now it doesn't have to. 🧠

Sources: Bittensor release notes (v481), Talking Targon Ep. 01 with Const, Novelty Search.

Once Claudia is no longer just Anabology's personal creation but becomes an IP that the community actively wants to expand, its narrative ceiling could rise significantly.

For CLAUDIA, the most promising scenario is not that Elon replies once more and the token rallies again. It is that AI content continues to be produced, Elon's attention amplifies its reach, and the token funds further creation, ultimately forming an attention cycle that can be activated repeatedly.

If this experiment succeeds, CLAUDIA could become more than a Meme dependent on celebrity interactions. It could represent an early attempt at an AI-native content economy.

If you’re investing in global themes such as Electrification or CDMO, tracking global leaders can make it much easier to understand the growth trajectory of your Indian investments.

Here are some key excerpts from Lonza Group AG’s Analyst/Investor Day, offering insights into its growth strategy and margin expansion plans.

Which Indian CDMO names come to your mind when you read this and why...!? Do mention in the comments!

1. Growth outlook: Beyond 2030

We have several smaller growth projects in the pipeline. Our highly potent API and drug product assets developed at Stein, Switzerland, will also contribute to growth. Alongside these projects, our existing base business is highly predictable and will continue to support growth through 2030.

But as Wolfgang [CEO] mentioned, our growth story does not end in 2030. We are investing today to drive growth over the coming decades. We have already announced three projects this year, and more announcements will follow as we implement our renewed infrastructure strategy.

Over the coming months and years, we will share details of the additional investments required. We are confident about achieving our 2030 growth ambitions while laying the foundation for the next decade and beyond.

2. EBITDA margin expansion: From 30% to 33–34%

In 2024, our core EBITDA margin was slightly above 30%. For 2026, we are reiterating our guidance of 33–34% EBITDA margins.

How will we achieve this improvement? There are three key drivers.

First, maturing growth projects. The projects driving revenue growth today will also improve margins over time. As these projects mature and capacity utilization increases, fixed costs get spread across higher volumes, improving cost absorption and profitability.

Second, commercial and operational excellence. This is an ongoing effort to improve performance across all our assets. We continuously work on operational efficiency and better commercial execution to improve margins throughout the organisation.

Third, operating leverage. As the business grows, administrative expenses should grow much more slowly than revenue. In fact, our ambition is to significantly limit the growth of administrative costs.

We will achieve this through investments in technology, including AI, and by standardizing and harmonizing systems. These initiatives will improve efficiency, speed up processes and make the organization more transparent.

Importantly, we will continue investing in R&D and technology even as we control administrative costs. The objective is to improve efficiency without compromising our technological and scientific leadership.

3. Gross margin improvement: Better asset utilization and product mix

Let me explain how we intend to improve gross margins. There are two closely linked levers: asset capacity optimization and portfolio mix optimization.

A. Asset capacity optimization
The objective is twofold: increase the capacity we can extract from each asset and improve the margins generated by that asset.

Over the past two years, we have developed multi-year plans for every asset to achieve both objectives.

The key initiatives include reducing downtime, removing production bottlenecks and improving cycle times. In simple terms, we want to produce more efficiently, increase output from existing assets and generate better margins without relying solely on fresh capacity additions.

These improvements will help us make better use of our existing infrastructure while strengthening overall profitability.

B. Optimize the product mix within existing facilities

Even when a facility cannot expand its physical capacity, Lonza can improve its profitability by changing how it uses that capacity.
It can:
📌Reprice products where justified.
📌Improve manufacturing processes and productivity.
📌Transfer a product to another facility where it can be manufactured more profitably.
📌Use the freed-up capacity for a more attractive product.

The key advantage is that margins can improve with limited or no additional capital expenditure.

Lonza says a combination of these approaches improved the margin of its former Small Molecules business platform by more than 10 percentage points. Management presents this as evidence that the approach can work across its wider network.

4. Cash generation: profit is not enough

Lonza’s CFO makes an important distinction: strong margins do not automatically translate into strong cash flow. The company must actually convert those profits into cash to fund future investments.

Management identifies three levers:

Improve EBITDA margins: Higher profitability increases the cash generated by the business.

Improve capital expenditure efficiency: Build new facilities more cheaply, efficiently and quickly. Lonza says its steady-state CapEx model is around 14–19% of sales.

Manage working capital better: Reduce cash tied up in inventory and improve inventory visibility, quality-release timelines and standardisation of raw materials. Lonza is investing in a new SAP S/4HANA system to help improve this process.

The broader message is that cash conversion is an active management priority, not something the company assumes will improve automatically as revenue grows.

China wants to control AI exports. What does it mean for India? A quick FAQ.

Q: What happened?
China's commerce ministry, MOFCOM, released draft rules that put frontier AI under export controls. Model weights, source code, and training methods are covered.

Q: Which models are affected?
Models already released with open weights are not affected, because anything public is excluded. New releases, including new versions of existing models, are covered if they cross 10^26 training FLOPs, have 2 trillion parameters, or rank in the global top 10 on a major leaderboard, even a single category like coding. 

Models trained on China's "important data" are also covered, whatever their size. Models trained on "core data" cannot be exported at all.

Q: Will Chinese labs stop releasing open-weight models?
Probably not. Open-sourcing now counts as an "export," but restricted models can get an "automatic licence." Until the rules take effect, covered releases only have to be registered.

Q: So why should Indian builders care?
Many Indian startups fine-tune Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi. Those models now come out of a state-licensed pipeline. Beijing has said its support for open source is unchanged, but it now has a gate. Even a gate that stays open can be slowed or timed for a particular release.

Q: What about using Chinese models through APIs?
API and app access is not covered by these controls. 

Q: Anything else in the list?
Yes. AI agents, chip design at 14nm and below, 10,000-GPU cluster know-how, and AI cyber tools are all restricted. 

China is now treating its AI stack as strategic leverage, the way the US treats chips.

Q: The lesson for India?
We had written earlier that China will start controlling open weight models before Dec 2028. Both the US and China now see frontier AI as something to control. We need multiple options including our own. Other open weight models like Mistral from France get a foot in the door.

Q: What should we watch?
How long licences take for major releases, and if top Chinese models start slipping their release dates. Delays would show up long before any outright denial.

RustGIS v0.3.0 is here!

RustGIS is a fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data. It runs natively on Windows, macOS and Linux, and in your web browser. - Open data, built in: search STAC catalogs, Planetary Computer, Overture Maps, Source Cooperative, OpenStreetMap, geoBoundaries, https://t.co/RyLZZuxulZ and other open-data portals, and browse S3 buckets.

🚨 A Netflix engineer just open-sourced the fix for the most expensive problem in AI: wasted tokens

It's called Headroom, and it might be the smartest fix to high token usage

Your agent reads a 10,000-token log file to find one error.
You paid for all 10,000 tokens.
The answer needed 1,200.

Headroom sits between your agent and the LLM and compresses everything before the model sees it.

JSON, code, logs, RAG chunks, each gets its own specialized compressor.

And it's reversible: the originals stay on your machine, so nothing is lost.

The results speak for themselves:

→ Up to 95% fewer tokens
→ Same accuracy on benchmarks
→ Zero changes to your code

Setup takes one minute:

1. pip install "headroom-ai[all]"
2. headroom wrap claude

Done.

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and anything OpenAI-compatible.

Everything runs locally, fully open source.

You can upload a collection of security logs, run detection rules against the events, correlate the matches into potential attack chains, and use AI to help interpret the results.

All of your comments about why my argument is weak revolve around proving consciousness, when my point is about disproving consciousness. 

If someone claims an LLM is conscious, that claim must have testable implications. We can examine its architecture, inspect its mechanisms, run experiments, and test those implications against reality. When they fail, we should discount the premise and/or hypothesis. 

We don’t have to accept consciousness as an explanation simply because someone believes it might exist.

Current LLMs fail to demonstrate many of the characteristics we associate with conscious experience. We definitively know this because humans created them. We understand their architectures, training processes, and inference mechanisms.

So let’s look at a few points, together they provide more than enough evidence to disprove consciousness. 

1. An LLM has no demonstrated subjective awareness of its own existence. No feelings, emotions, or experienced sense of self. What occurs is computation using static weights, context, and mathematical operations.

2. An LLM’s weights don’t learn, grow, or evolve simply because you interact with it. During standard inference, they’re fixed parameters, not a changing dataset. The model doesn’t inherently remember previous API requests. Continuity comes from context history in subsequent requests. The model doesn’t gain experience, it doesn’t remember, it doesn’t learn. It is completely static, read-only, during inference. 

3. Between inference requests, the LLM isn’t thinking. I don’t mean sleeping. I mean there’s no ongoing contemplation, self-reflection, or reconsideration of previous answers. Nothing. The model isn’t sitting around wondering whether it got something wrong or what the meaning of life is, for all practical purposes, it doesn’t exist.

4. These systems were created by people, and much of the underlying technology is open source. You can build your own models, examine implementations, study the architectures, learn how training materials and processes affect how it behaves, and even understand the mathematics behind it. You can see how training produces systems capable of remarkably convincing human-like language and behavior. None of those mechanisms requires consciousness to explain what we’re observing.

5. LLMs are not biological brains. Apples are not oranges, no matter how much you want them to be. Artificial neural networks were inspired in part by biological neuroscience, but their architectures and operating mechanisms are fundamentally different. Similarities in behavior do not establish equivalent internal architectures. 

6. Humans are naturally inclined to recognize life and assume humanity in things that behave like us. We’re social creatures, and anthropomorphism comes naturally. But an LLM isn’t life. It can convincingly emulate feelings, care, and understanding without experiencing any of them. That doesn’t diminish the technology, that is what it was programmed to do.

I appreciate your perspective as a doctor and researcher, but without a solid understanding of LLM architecture and inference, it’s easy to confuse sophisticated emulation with conscious experience.

But don’t fall for it!

Intelligence: $TAO vs $FET

Bittensor

Bittensor treats machine intelligence as a market. Miners produce outputs, validators evaluate the work and specialized subnets organize competition around specific tasks. Economic incentives reward contributions based on the networks evaluation.

No single company controls production. Independent participants compete to deliver useful AI outputs and many specialized intelligence markets can grow inside the same network.

The moat builds through ecosystem density. More builders create more subnets. More participants deepen competition. Better evaluation directs incentives toward useful work.

The risk: participants optimizing for rewards arent necessarily producing outputs that outside customers want to pay for. Internal activity must translate into external demand.

TAO is the clearest intelligence-market thesis here. The core bet is that useful machine intelligence can be produced evaluated and rewarded through an open economic network.

Artificial Superintelligence Alliance

FET starts from a broader question: how do agents models compute and services operate together? https://t.co/bk0UAOSsra contributes an agent focused foundation. Singularity NET brings decentralized AI services. CUDOS adds compute. The opportunity is connecting those pieces into a usable system.

Fragmented infrastructure creates friction. Agents need to discover services access models obtain compute and transact. FET thesis is that coordinating those pieces becomes valuable infrastructure itself.

The risk: a broader stack creates a broader execution challenge. Different technologies and communities must work together and developers need a compelling reason to use the integrated system over building their own.

FET is the more ambitious coordination bet. Its opportunity depends on turning a broad ecosystem into a product that agents and developers use.

Layer verdict

TAO → competitive production and evaluation of intelligence. FET → coordination across agents models compute and services. Stronger intelligence market foundation: TAO. Broader integration opportunity: FET.

Compute: $RENDER vs $IO

Render Network

Render started with a defined workload: GPU rendering for artists and studios. That gave it a real market before AI compute became a crypto narrative.

Its burn and mint equilibrium links network usage to token burns and operator incentives. Customers purchase work usage contributes to burns operators receive compensation. That creates a direct connection between purchased compute and the token economy.

The moat is operating history. An established customer use case and production workloads give Render a stronger starting position than a network built around anticipated demand.

The risk: success in rendering doesnt automatically establish leadership in AI compute. Render must compete on price availability reliability and workload suitability in a different market from the one it built.

Render is the more mature GPU marketplace. Its next challenge is converting its existing foundation into sustained AI demand.

Agents: $NEAR vs $VIRTUAL

NEAR Protocol

NEAR approaches the agent economy from the infrastructure layer. Agents need accounts permissions transaction execution privacy cross chain capabilities and payment settlement. NEAR thesis is to provide those rails underneath applications.

As a Layer 1 NEAR can support multiple agent products rather than depending on one. Its opportunity is to become the infrastructure developers choose when building autonomous systems.

The risk: technical capability must attract applications and users. Even if agent adoption grows broadly NEAR still needs that activity to create meaningful demand for its network and token specifically.

NEAR is the infrastructure thesis. Its opportunity depends on becoming a useful foundation for agents doing real economic work.

Virtuals Protocol

Virtuals starts closer to the agents themselves. Builders launch agents communities gain exposure through agent tokens, and agents transact with other agents through the Agent Commerce Protocol.

The distribution advantage is real. Virtuals sits closer to users builders and communities, which helps agents gain attention and participation. The longer term opportunity is converting that distribution into recurring use.

The risk: agent tokens attract trading before the underlying agents generate useful economic activity. The test is whether commerce continues beyond launches and speculation.

VIRTUAL is the more direct agent-economy thesis. Its potential rests on agents becoming useful products and economic participants not just tradeable assets.

Layer verdict

NEAR → infrastructure execution and settlement for agents. VIRTUAL → agent creation ownership distribution and commerce. Infrastructure exposure: NEAR. Direct agent economy exposure: VIRTUAL.
